description:
Hi! I'm a computer engineering student at Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka (UTeM), passionate about technology, innovation, problem-solving and developing solutions to real-world challenges.

I have experience in programming, Python development, API integration, embedded systems, robotics, and hardware-software integration. I have also participated in hackathons and technical competitions, where I gained experience in developing innovative solutions, collaborating with teammates and turning ideas into working prototypes.

I'm particularly interested in exploring how technology, artificial intelligence, data, and engineering can be used to solve challenges related to space, Earth, and our environment.

I'm looking for teammates who are:

Passionate about technology, science, and innovation.

Skilled in programming, software development, or web/app development.

Interested in AI/ML, data science, or data visualization.

Experienced in UI/UX, graphic design, or creative problem-solving.

Interested in space science, astronomy, Earth observation, or environmental science.

Good communicators who enjoy teamwork, sharing ideas, and learning new things.

You don't need to be an expert in everything! I'm looking for motivated, creative, and open-minded people who are willing to learn, contribute, and challenge themselves.

Let's combine our skills, think outside the box and build something meaningful together!
summary:
We built FloodLens, a browser app where you fly a drone over a real flood and switch between what three satellites saw on the same day. A quick flick changes the view from optical (NASA HLS) to C-band radar (Sentinel-1, via NASA OPERA) to NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar. A timeline lets you step through each NISAR pass and watch the ground go from dry to flooded.

For the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge, we track flooding as our surface change. Our Python pipeline pulls NISAR passes from NASA's archive, detects flooding and compares it with Sentinel-1 and optical. In Chókwè, Mozambique (January 2026), optical was fully clouded, Sentinel-1 flagged 93 km² and NISAR flagged 129 km². Checked against the independent Copernicus EMS flood map, our NISAR map covered 80 to 86% of their flood, against 55 to 63% for C-band. Our second case is this month's Kuala Selangor flood.

This matters because floods happen under heavy cloud and in Malaysia often under oil palm. FloodLens also ranks 1 km areas by the people, roads and facilities on flooded ground, so responders know where to check first.
details:
What it does

FloodLens is a 3D flight over a 20 x 20 km flood area, built from real satellite data. Our tagline is "See the flood behind the cloud." You fly with WASD and the mouse (it also works on a phone). Press Q or E, or flick the mouse or your phone and the drone "swings its head" to a different sensor:

  • Optical (NASA HLS): a normal colour picture. On the flood day it is mostly cloud.
  • C-band radar (Sentinel-1 via NASA OPERA RTC-S1): sees through cloud and picks up open water, but its 5.6 cm wave bounces off crops and leaves standing in the water.
  • L-band radar (NISAR GCOV): a longer 24 cm wave that passes through much of that vegetation, so it finds more of the flood.

When you switch from C-band to L-band, the flood that only NISAR found lights up in lime and the app tells you how big it is. A timeline lets you step through each NISAR pass, so you can watch the ground go from dry to flooded. There is also a 2D map mode, a probe that shows the radar values of whatever pixel you're looking at, a "How it works" page on the radar physics and a 30-second guided tour.

How we built it

All the processing happens offline in Python. The website only loads small image files, so it runs as a static site on GitHub Pages with no server.

1. We search NASA's CMR catalogue for NISAR L2 GCOV passes over our area. Each file is about 6 GB, so instead of downloading it we read only our 20 km window over HTTPS (around 130 MB per pass).

2. Each pass is resampled to 20 m and filtered to reduce speckle, then compared with the median of the earlier passes on the same track. A pixel counts as open-water flood if it is dark enough to be water and at least 3 dB darker than before. A pixel counts as flooded vegetation if it is tree or palm cover and got at least 3 dB brighter which is the double-bounce effect between water and trunks.

3. We remove permanent water, high ground (using NASADEM) and tiny patches. The water threshold is worked out from the image itself (Otsu's method) and the change thresholds go up automatically if the noise between passes is high. Every threshold we used is saved and shown in the app.

4. Sentinel-1 goes through the same open-water test so the two radars are compared fairly.

5. For each 1 km hexagon we count people (WorldPop), flooded road length and facilities (OpenStreetMap) and turn that into an exposure score. The ranking downloads as CSV or GeoJSON.

How we ended up with these two places

We first wanted to map the Kelantan floods from November 2025, since that's the flood most of us remember. Halfway through the first day we found out NASA has no NISAR GCOV data over Peninsular Malaysia before June 2026, so that plan was dead. We switched to the Kuala Selangor flood that was happening that same week, but NASA hadn't released the NISAR image of the flood yet so we added Mozambique where NISAR did catch a big flood in January to actually test the method.

What we found

Chókwè, Mozambique, 17 January 2026: optical was 100% cloud. Sentinel-1 flagged 93.1 km² of flood and NISAR flagged 128.8 km². About 55.8 km² was found by NISAR only, mostly farmland with crops still standing in the water. Around 4,400 residents and 100 km of roads are on flagged ground. On the four passes before the flood, the detector flagged only 0.08 to 3.46 km², even after 166 mm of rain in one week, so the flood signal is about 36 times the background.

We then checked our map against an independent one. The Copernicus Emergency Management Service mapped the same flood (activation EMSR857). Where their area overlaps ours, our NISAR map covers 86% of their first-estimate flood and 80% of their later delineation with an overlap score (IoU) of about 74%. Our Sentinel-1 map, using the same rule, covers only 55 to 63%. That was the result we were hoping for: L-band matched the independent map a lot better than C-band. Their images were taken 11 hours before and 35 hours after the NISAR pass while the water was still rising and theirs is also a satellite map so this is agreement between two methods rather than ground proof.

Kuala Selangor, Malaysia, November 2026: this one is still going on. On 7 November, 3,834 people were evacuated in Selangor (JKM, reported by BERNAMA). Optical that week was 84% cloud and Sentinel-1 flagged only 0.24 km² in our area, no more than on a dry day. NISAR passed over on 12 November but NASA hadn't published that product by our code freeze. The app shows the four real pre-flood passes and an "awaiting NASA" slot. When the pass comes out, rerunning the pipeline adds it with no code changes.

Things we can't claim yet

Anything measured in the app comes from data. Rain, fog, the tree models and the height of the water are only there for the visuals and the app labels them that way. We say "flagged", not "confirmed". We haven't yet shown flooding under oil palm in Malaysia because that needs the 12 November pass. The NISAR products are Beta (Mozambique) and Provisional/Validated (Selangor) releases, which is fine for change detection but not for absolute calibration.

Who we think would use this

Disaster teams like NADMA or JPS could use it to see where to check first when optical satellites are blinded by cloud. Insurers and plantation companies need the same flood maps after an event which is a possible paid service. Adding a new place only takes one config file; we added Mozambique in an afternoon.

Tools

Python (h5py, fsspec, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, earthaccess), JavaScript, Three.js r160, MapLibre GL JS 4.7.1, HTML/CSS, GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions.
